extracted.intended_audience: administrative law practitioners, CPP administrators, appeals officers, and legal scholars studying CPP procedures
extracted.subtask_description: Procedure and substantive rules governing determinations, appeals, sanctions, decision-making bodies, and Review Committees under the Canada Pension Plan (CPP), including fact-gathering, report drafting, timelines, criminal and administrative penalties, and composition/formation of Review Committees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to submit representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals and business firms directly involved in a case will avail themselves of the right to submit representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties often retain lawyers to draft representations. Representations submitted by one party are not divulged to other parties unless they appear difficult to reconcile, in which case the official may organize a confrontation between the parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officials' fact-finding powers and duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Section officials may hear parties in person and take a personal part in proceedings, and possess the same power to investigate cases and to compel production of documents as Rulings Officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the CPP they are obliged to proceed 'with all due dispatch' in fact-finding and are expected to be familiar with and take into account previous determinations, PAB jurisprudence, and relevant common law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report drafting requirement for determination
rubrics_metrics.description: At the end of fact-gathering the official in charge drafts a report outlining the facts, his evaluation of the facts, and the caselaw and legal rules applicable to the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report must receive approval of the head of the Determinations and Appeals Section before the decision is transmitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of communication of determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions are transmitted to the parties by the Director of Legal Services (Taxation) by means of a form-letter which draws attention to the right of appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The form-letter confines itself to stating briefly the solution to the question raised, without detailing facts, law, or reasons. Except for the right of appeal, the determination is final and binding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical timeline for determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Approximately three months will elapse between the time a determination is requested and the date it is delivered to the parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the normal course of events stated for the period surveyed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and definition of an assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: An assessment is the act whereby the Department of National Revenue claims from an employer payment of the contribution corresponding to an employee in his business firm; it is issued for the total amount due and includes employer and employee portions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments are the administrative instrument being challenged via determination/appeal mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for challenging an assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessments may be challenged on two grounds: (1) the amount of contributions assessed, and (2) whether any contribution is payable (coverage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience indicates appeals are roughly equally divided between these two types of challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limit to institute an appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals must be instituted within 90 days from the date of the assessment (period for appeals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The procedural formalities for instituting appeals are virtually indistinguishable from determinations except for this time limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural parity of determinations and appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: The processes of determination and appeal are virtually indistinguishable: formalities of initiating, examining the case, and formulating a decision apply mutatis mutandis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sole significant procedural difference noted is the time allowed for instituting the processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two types of sanctions (criminal vs administrative)
rubrics_metrics.description: CPP sanctions are of two types: criminal sanctions (forming part of general criminal law) and administrative sanctions (peculiar to administrative law and enforceable against property only).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative sanctions are applied by administrative authorities and may be executed against property; criminal sanctions may include imprisonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal offences under section 42 — list
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 42(4) provides penalties against: any action with intent to evade compliance or payment of contributions; any false or deceptive statements in fulfillment of requirements under the Act; falsification, alteration, or destruction of employer records to evade payment; and any conspiracy to commit the foregoing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subsections (1)–(3) create specific offences with additional special sanctions beyond (4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal penalties and sentencing ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: Offenders under section 42 may be liable to fines from $25 to $5,000 plus, where appropriate, an amount not exceeding double the amount of the contribution evaded or attempted to be evaded; imprisonment up to six months may also apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penalties under subsections (1)–(3) may differ and section 115 of the Criminal Code may apply for certain offences (e.g., failure to keep books) with longer imprisonment (two years).

rubrics_metrics.name: No intent required for many offences
rubrics_metrics.description: The element of intent is not necessary for every offence under section 42; false or deceptive statements or written representations may be offences even if made in good faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere non-compliance in good faith with many provisions suffices to render the individual liable to criminal action; administrative sanctions likewise often apply without fraudulent intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary conviction procedure and prosecutorial authority
rubrics_metrics.description: All offences under section 42 are to be prosecuted according to the summary procedure in Part XXIV of the Criminal Code; Inspectors of the Department of National Revenue have authority to initiate proceedings themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision to institute prosecutions under section 42 is not subject to control by the PAB; only regular criminal courts rule on accusation validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sections providing administrative penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative penalties (in the form of 'penalties') are provided by sections 22 (employers), 36 (self-employed individuals), 41 (applicable to all contributors), and section 42 (relationship between criminal and administrative sanctions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These sections set out different penalty regimes tailored to the offender category and the nature of the default.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 22(6) employer penalty for late remittance
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 22(6) imposes on the defaulting employer a penalty of 10% of the amount outstanding for failing to remit sums representing his and employees' contributions by the prescribed date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This penalty is distinct from interest due on the debt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 36(1) self-employed penalty for late filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 36(1) makes a self-employed individual who fails to file a statement of earnings within the prescribed time liable to a penalty amounting to 5% of the balance of his contribution still outstanding as of the filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Minister may remit the penalty in whole or in part if a penalty has already been imposed under the Income Tax Act for the same year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 36(2) agents/trustees penalty
rubrics_metrics.description: Agents, trustees and assignees called upon to file a statement for a self-employed individual who fails to do so incur a penalty of $5 for each day of default, not exceeding $50 in all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This penalty is far less severe than that imposed on the principal self-employed individual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 41(1) regulation-making penalty power
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 41(1) delegates to the Governor in Council the power to make regulations prescribing submission/transmission of information and may prescribe penalties not exceeding $10 a day, up to $250, for failure to file or transmit such information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections 200–205 of the CPP Regulations were established under this provision and fix the penalty at the maximum provided by the CPP.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collection and challenge of penalties as assessment debt
rubrics_metrics.description: Penalties are collectible by the same right and means as contributions; they are included in the amount of the assessment transmitted by the Minister and constitute a debt to the Crown recoverable in Federal Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imposition of a penalty may be challenged before the PAB by lodging an appeal against a notice of assessment, though such a challenge appears not to have been attempted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship and order of application between criminal and administrative sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 42 provides that imposition of criminal sanctions will not preclude administrative sanctions, but subsection (5) specifies that administrative sanctions cannot be added to criminal sanctions unless the payment of the penalty was demanded before the information or complaint giving rise to the conviction was laid or made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This suggests the legislator intended administrative sanctions as the first instrument of enforcement, to be used prior to criminal sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision-making structure for CPP benefits — centralization and delegation
rubrics_metrics.description: Decision-making for CPP benefits is exercised at three successive levels: units of the Department of National Health and Welfare, the Minister (Director General acting by delegation), and the Review Committees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within the Department the Director General acts under delegated authority and exercises principal powers conferred on the Minister under Parts II and III; Regional Services Division and three central units (CB, DA, Appeals) play direct roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: District offices' role in claims processing
rubrics_metrics.description: District offices act as a clearing house for applications: assist applicants in filing, explain procedures, identify needed documents, distribute application forms, and ensure each applicant's file is complete before forwarding to the General Directorate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agents also publicize the plan, provide information to the public, and organize sittings of Review Committees (often on their premises).

rubrics_metrics.name: Local offices' function and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Local offices are small units served by travelling agents intended to save applicants travel costs by providing local information and assistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A drawback is potential delay due to infrequent visits by travelling agents, which may cause applicants who insist on in-person discussion to face delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims and Benefits Division (CB) decision standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The Claims and Benefits Division has full authority to decide all applications for benefits except disability-specific aspects; decisions mainly involve verifying whether objective statutory conditions of eligibility are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Difficulties arise where statutory conditions are doubtful or when discretionary powers under section 63 are invoked; CB also supervises ongoing eligibility conditions (widowhood, dependency, attendance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disability Assessment Division (DA) expertise requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: DA settles questions of disability raised by benefit applications and requires special (chiefly medical) qualifications to appreciate eligibility, including physicians, nurses, and rehabilitation specialists; it consults private specialists when needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because duration is critical to disability determinations, DA must provide sustained supervision and monitoring, making greater time demands on staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals Section procedural and liaison role
rubrics_metrics.description: The Appeals Section does not exercise decision-making power but ensures correct conduct of procedure at the first two levels of appeal and liaises between beneficiaries, district offices, central units (CB or DA), and Review Committees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It coordinates participation of central units in the appeal process and acknowledges appeals by letter outlining general procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review Committees' composition and status
rubrics_metrics.description: Review Committees are ad hoc 'people's appeal tribunals' constituted of members designated equally by the litigants and a third chairman coopted by the two members or designated by a superior court judge; members must be Canadian residents and committees have no permanent infrastructure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their essential features are set out in section 84; they may sit in any convenient place and their composition depends on parties' will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation process and timing of Review Committees
rubrics_metrics.description: Formation generally devolves on the district office within the appellant's territory; the process often begins with designation, within fifteen days of receiving notice of appeal, of a secretary and of the committee member appointed by the Minister.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In spouse-right appeals (where appellants may be distant) the Appeals Section organizes the Committee; appellants are expected to identify their chosen member when giving notice but often do so after acknowledgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection criteria and exclusion for Review Committee members
rubrics_metrics.description: Service instructions require selecting individuals whose impartiality is above suspicion; officials of the Department of National Health and Welfare and federal civil servants are barred from appointment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred categories include businessmen, retired professionals, social club directors, provincial/municipal supervisory officials, ministers of religion, school trustees, self-employed individuals, and housewives with relevant experience.
